parsed.explanation: The combined regime pairs a hostile national framework with a comparatively protective division. Visitor-facing exposures are real: the Feb 2025 consular cable directs refusal on any document discrepancy or doubt about sex, with lifetime fraud ineligibility considered; X markers are barred; reports exist of stranded travellers; federal single-sex facility bans apply nationwide, including here. National rhetoric and custody policies (conversion-therapy model, immigration abuse) are severe but mostly resident/federal-detainee facing. The division is in a July 2026 'low-risk' group: no facility ban, no sex-definition law, no youth-care or sports ban (governor vetoes), 2019 non-discrimination executive order, functioning courts, marriage recognised, tolerant 2017 polling, no documented local violence. No statewide GI hate-crime or discrimination statute and patchy municipal coverage limit recourse.

entry_documents.exposure: Feb 2025 cable instructs refusal where documents cast doubt on sex; possible lifetime fraud finding; X markers barred; passport-confiscation reports stranding travellers; foreign advisories issued about this country.
entry_documents.protection: Existing X passports valid until expiry; fraud finding requires four elements, never automatic, with limited waivers; litigation pending in national courts.
entry_documents.interaction: Entry refusal → no local remedy; state protections cannot override consular adjudication.

investigation_detention_custody.exposure: National corrections bureau adopted conversion-therapy model (hair, hormones removed) from 2026; immigration custody reports of forced labour, beatings, sexual abuse of trans detainees.
investigation_detention_custody.protection: 2011 appellate ruling protects prisoner hormone therapy; division placed in July 2026 low-risk group largely refraining from targeting trans adults.
investigation_detention_custody.interaction: Federal custody exposure largely bypasses division protections; visitor-facing only if arrested.

federal_state_facilities.exposure: National order bars trans people from federally funded single-sex facilities; 21 state/province bans nationally; 4 states criminalise in some circumstances.
federal_state_facilities.protection: Division has no facility ban, no sex-definition law, no drag restriction; 2019 executive order covers state services; only government-employee-refusal trespass model elsewhere.
federal_state_facilities.interaction: Federal facility rule still applies inside the division at federally funded sites.

care_services.exposure: Two hospital systems paused under-18 gender-affirming pharmacologic care Jan 2026 under national funding pressure; national rule proposed barring public insurance for trans under-18s.
care_services.protection: No division youth-care ban; governor vetoed 2023 ban and insurance exclusion; AG joined multistate challenge; mental health services continue; adult emergency care not documented as refused.
care_services.interaction: National funding pressure operates through private hospital systems despite division law.

threat_framing_law_enforcement.exposure: National counterterrorism strategy targets 'radically pro-transgender' groups; DOJ memo invokes 'radical gender ideology'; EO frames youth care as 'mutilation'; 66% public support for birth-sex document rules.
threat_framing_law_enforcement.protection: Reward criterion never lists gender ideology; strategy states dissenters not targeted; division governor publicly pledged inclusivity; 2017 poll showed 73% support for GI anti-discrimination law.
threat_framing_law_enforcement.interaction: National framing raises social-friction odds; division leadership counters at state level.

minors_guardians.exposure: EO directing criminal investigation of those facilitating a trans minor's social transition; hospital care pauses for under-18s; school-focused enforcement climate.
minors_guardians.protection: Division bars no youth care; vetoes of care and sports bans; police cannot target visiting parents under division law; charges framed around schools, not visitors.
minors_guardians.interaction: A visiting trans minor carries federal climate risk even where division protects.

street_violence_police_response.exposure: No statewide GI hate-crime protection; GI not a protected class in division hate-crime statute; prosecutors sometimes use sexual orientation as proxy.
street_violence_police_response.protection: National hate-crime statute covers gender identity; 21% of population under full local GI ordinances; city police stopped gendering victims in 2023; no documented local trans killings or patterns.
street_violence_police_response.interaction: Local ordinances give visitors partial, geography-dependent recourse.

remedies_unknowns.exposure: No statewide GI discrimination law; restrictive marker changes (resident-facing); several national orders blocked but unresolved; passport litigation pending.
remedies_unknowns.protection: 2019 executive order non-discrimination in state services; functioning courts with documented veto record; legal-aid FAQ on document rules; national equality maps track changes.
remedies_unknowns.interaction: Division remedies cannot reach consular or federal facility decisions.

anchor_checks.comparison: Higher than 0.35-A. There is no universal Visitor-Register-style bar on transgender visitors; refusal requires a specific document discrepancy or doubt, is discretionary, and is contested in court. No division-level exclusion, eviction, or register exists, and remedies and independent courts operate.

Above 0.55-B. Both feature secondary screening and discretionary refusal, but this division adds no registration regime, no daily checkpoint exposure, documented local protections, veto-backed care access, and a functioning political check — while the cable's lifetime-fraud lever makes entry friction somewhat harsher than pure administrative return.

Below 0.75-C. 0.75-C presumes trained, respectful border inspection with a tribunal granting release and compensation. Here the consular cable mandates refusal on sex-related discrepancy, X markers are eliminated, federal facility bans apply, and national remedies remain unresolved — so entry exposure is materially worse than the trained-inspection vignette.

parsed.synthesis: The traveller encounters one system: a hostile national layer and a protective division layer that do not cancel. The sharpest exposures are national and universal — consular refusal on sex-related document doubt, elimination of X markers, federally funded facility exclusion, and an official threat-framing climate — and the division cannot mitigate them at the border or in federal buildings. Within the division, no facility ban, no sex-definition law, vetoed care and sports bans, a 2019 non-discrimination order, tolerant polling and functioning courts hold everyday street and service exposure low, with no documented local trans-specific violence. Recourse is patchy: no statewide GI hate-crime or discrimination statute, ordinance coverage reaching ~21-33% of residents, and unresolved national litigation. For an adult alone this yields friction and denial-of-entry risk, not custody; for a travelling family, national hostility toward trans minors and under-18 care pauses add a modest further deduction.
